newsitem.title: NORWAY: LOW PAPER PRICE WEAKENS NORSKE SKOG PROFITS.
newsitem.headline: LOW PAPER PRICE WEAKENS NORSKE SKOG PROFITS.

text.p: Norway's largest forestry group, Norske Skogindustrier ASA , on Wednesday announced weaker first-quarter results than in the same year-ago period because of low printing paper prices.
Norske Skog made a pre-tax profit of 118 million crowns in the first quarter of 1997, down from 602 million.

"The trend of results reflects the fact that printing paper prices so far this year have been significantly lower than in January-March 1996. The markets for pulp remain weak," the company said in a statement.
The group's operating revenue fell to 2.86 billion crowns from 3.49 billion, operating profits shrank to 170 million from 654 million and the after-tax result dropped to 85 million from 429 million.

"Demand for printing paper is stable. Prices for SC magazine paper and newsprint are expected to remain stable, but at a low level. Some rise in prices is expected for pulp and LWC magazine paper," the statement said.
"For sawn timber, demand on European export markets is expected to continue to be good. However, the strong Norwegian crown eliminates much of the price rise," it said.
The group's equity capital ratio stood at 46 percent at the end of the first quarter.
The first-quarter result fell short of market expectations.
From the New Year, newsprint prices fell by 15-20 percent, and they will probably remain at this level for the rest of this year in Western Europe, Norske Skog said.
From first quarter 1996 to first quarter 1997, the price decline was between 20 and 25 percent.
"So far, there has been some improvement in demand for newsprint in the United States, and prices have risen somewhat. That should have a positive impact in Europe, too, next year," it said.

Demand for SC magazine paper is better than in the same period last year, but prices declined by 15 percent in January. From first quarter 1996 to first quarter 1997, prices declined by 25-30 percent.

"We expect prices to remain stable for the rest of 1997. For LWC magazine paper, the favourable trend of demand seen during the second half of 1996 has continued during the first quarter of 1997, and prices are now rising somewhat.
Pulp markets weakened further during the first quarter, leading to large stocks and continued price declines, it said.
It said supply and demand on the sawn timber market in Europe was now better balanced than it was during 1996.
"Stocks of sawn timber are low in Scandinavia, and this should pave the way for a further rise in prices," Norske Skog said.
